source.title: How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
source.authors: Lin Chen; Bo-Lin Ni; Qi Yang; Lan Jiang; Kun Ding; Xiao-Ran Fan; Hower Yang; Ying Wang; Shi-Ming Xiang

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present, though some figure and table layouts are flattened in the web extraction
record.tranche_reason: It extends scaling-law measurements to encoder-free versus encoder-based multimodal language-model pretraining, while also measuring text-objective scaling in the same model ladder.
record.gate_note: Rows cover held-out validation-loss scaling, compute-optimal allocations, held-out forecasts, fitting/accounting sensitivity, and downstream benchmark trends. The paper also reports internal attention, representation, and routing probes, but those do not measure the claim versions. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It fits IsoFLOP loss–compute and allocation laws on held-out validation loss for a matched sparse-MoE MLLM ladder, for both text and image-conditioned objectives. It checks held-out forecasts and varies estimator, irreducible-loss floor and compute accounting. This is a new setting (multimodal MoE, encoder-free vs encoder-based) with its own results on V1, V2, V3, V5, V6 and V7. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors add that the visual-encoder prior's advantage diminishes with scale. Their decoder-probe findings (bidirectional visual attention, earlier visual processing, concentrated routing) are interpretation, not claim-relevant results.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IsoFLOP profiles and compute-optimal allocation analysis associated with prior scaling-law work, but applies them to a matched sparse-MoE multimodal ladder, uses held-out validation losses for separate text and image-conditioned objectives, and compares encoder-free against encoder-based systems with a fixed visual encoder.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss–compute exponents and crossover vary with the assumed irreducible-loss floor; the encoder-based allocation and loss exponent change when visual-encoder FLOPs are included. The envelope estimator gives allocation and loss exponents close to IsoFLOP estimates. Causal versus bidirectional visual attention changes the fitted allocation exponents only slightly. Topic and overtraining factor also change the projected multimodal crossover.

fits_no_version.finding: Encoder-free vs encoder-based equal-loss efficiency and extrapolated crossover (~6.1e21 FLOPs compute-optimal, 1.2e22 at 5× overtraining); overtraining lowers EGC 0.62→0.52 and EGM 0.80→0.74.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing a pretrained visual encoder costs compute at small scale but the gap shrinks with scale in MLLM pretraining.

record.problems: The principal fits use six logarithmically spaced budgets per objective, covering approximately one decade of compute. The crossover is extrapolated beyond the measured range and assumes fitted laws persist, a fixed visual-encoder size, and a shared irreducible loss. The authors state that fitted exponents and crossover are sensitive to the irreducible-loss specification. The downstream figure gives no fitted prediction law. Some figure-only downstream values and parts of the flattened benchmark table are not recoverable as exact per-condition values from the extracted text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 6 reports individual benchmark scores across six model sizes and two architectures; these per-benchmark cells were not extracted because they exceed the 60-row limit, while the table layout is flattened and the aggregate downstream trend is retained in r24. Other reported internal attention, representation, and expert-routing analyses do not bear on the claim versions.

untested.parts: Separate loss-vs-parameter and loss-vs-token laws; ranges of several orders of magnitude (fits span about one decade); dense non-MoE models.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude; only 5× (text) and 2.5× (multimodal) were tested.
Allocation by parameter count (the study uses FLOPs/token in MoE); dense models.
Entire version; depth and width are not isolated at fixed size.
Video, pure image models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer.
Any quantitative prediction of downstream scores from scale or loss.
Curvature away from a power law at larger scales; parameter-counting and schedule choices; cross-literature disagreement.

missing.what: Envelope-estimator text exponents: a=0.430/0.435 and γ=0.0905/0.0915, vs IsoFLOP 0.427/0.422 and 0.0973/0.0979.
Envelope multimodal loss exponents γ=0.3668/0.3050 vs IsoFLOP 0.3778/0.2998.
Per-topic allocation exponents: text topics differ ≤0.004 between architectures; multimodal topics a≈0.40–0.59.

record.verdict_notes: Fits cover about one decade of compute, with six budgets per objective. M is FLOPs/token in a fixed-ratio MoE, so allocation exponents are not directly parameter-count exponents. Reader's V2/V5 limits_scope labels for untested ranges and modalities were moved to untested. Rows r21–r23 were unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits compute-optimal loss against training compute for text and multimodal objectives; it does not report separate held-out loss-versus-parameter and loss-versus-token laws with the other quantities held non-bottlenecked.
Held-out forecasts test 5× extrapolation for text and 2.5× for multimodal loss, not forecasts across orders of magnitude.
Reports fitted parameter and token allocation exponents for the tested objectives and architectures; it does not test all training setups or establish a universal allocation law.
The comparison changes the visual front end and attention pattern; it does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests image-conditioned multimodal pretraining in this MLLM setup, not image or video models generally, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports downstream benchmark averages against compute and scores at about 100B tokens; it does not fit or validate a quantitative downstream prediction law.

Tests estimator, irreducible-loss, and compute-accounting choices in this study; it does not test whether curves bend away from a power law at much larger scales or explain disagreements across the full literature.
